conceptTag: Your biggest customer wants a custom feature
readerTitle: Your biggest customer wants something only they will use
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (레스토랑 그룹에 주방 재고 소프트웨어를 파는 회사) · 모든 인물, 수치, 사건은 설명용
insight: 큰 고객의 맞춤 요청은 받아 적을 주문이 아니라 하나의 구매 결정이다. 누가 원하고, 누가 쓰고, 누가 서명하는지, 그리고 그들이 무엇을 위험으로 느끼는지부터 본다.
misconception: 가장 큰 고객이 요청하면 무엇이든, 무료로라도 그대로 만들어 주는 것이 관계를 지키는 길이다.

sources.text: 이 유닛(CUS-09)의 개념: 구매자와 사용자, 구매 위원회, 기업 구매의 위험, 총소유비용, 신뢰와 관계
모든 수치와 사건은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(매출 비중 30%, 40개 매장, 고객 200곳, 개발 6주, 2주 지연)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 모든 시나리오 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
'나쁜 소식을 일찍 전하면 신뢰가 더 쌓일 수 있다'는 표현은 일반적인 관찰로만 썼습니다. 서비스 회복 역설(CUS-06-05) 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다. 단정적 표현으로 바꾸지 마세요.
알레르기 관리는 국가마다 법적 요건이 다릅니다. 레슨은 법률 조언이 아니며, 특정 규제를 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your biggest customer wants something only they will use
body: You run a small company that makes kitchen inventory software for restaurants. One customer, a 40-location restaurant group, brings in 30% of your revenue.
Their operations director emails: *"We need a custom allergen dashboard built for us. Our contract renews in three months."*

image.label: A founder reading an urgent email from a restaurant group
image.brief: 작은 사무실에서 노트북 화면의 이메일을 읽는 창업자. 화면 옆에 레스토랑 주방 사진, 달력에는 3개월 뒤 'Renewal' 표시. 긴장감 있는 따뜻한 일러스트. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: The email lands. What's your first move?
body: Your team could build the dashboard in about six weeks. None of your other 200 restaurant customers has asked for it.

options.text: Reply yes today and start building
options.feedback: You keep the mood warm, but you're building to a description, not a problem. Six weeks of work may solve the wrong thing.

options.text: Ask to talk with the director, two kitchen managers and whoever signs the renewal
options.feedback: It costs a week. In return you learn who wants this, who will use it, and who actually decides.

options.text: Politely decline: you don't build custom features
options.feedback: It protects your product, but you've said no before knowing what's behind the request. Your biggest customer hears "we don't listen."

cards.title: Say you chose to ask. Three people, three wants.
body: A guest at one location had an allergic reaction last month. The director wants a dashboard to show the board. The kitchen managers want something simpler: allergen flags on each recipe and printed labels on prep containers. The finance director, who signs, wants the price not to rise.

options.text: The full custom dashboard, free, to secure the renewal
options.feedback: You win the room, then maintain a one-off forever. Every future update must keep it working, and nobody pays you for that.

options.text: Allergen flags and labels as a standard feature for every customer, plus a simple summary report for the director
options.feedback: Cooks get what they'll use, the director gets something to show, and your other customers get it too. One build, many payers.

options.text: The full dashboard, priced as a custom project
options.feedback: Honest about cost, but finance wanted no price rise. And you still own the upkeep long after the project fee is spent.

cards.title: Say you chose the standard feature. Finance hesitates.
body: The finance director says: *"A rival already offers allergen tracking. Why should we wait for yours?"* Switching would be a big job for her team, but she has to defend this choice to the board.

options.feedback: It lowers her cost but not her worry: what if your feature doesn't work? You give up margin and leave the real problem unsolved.

options.text: Offer a pilot in five locations, with a clear yes-or-no date before renewal
options.feedback: It shrinks her risk. She doesn't bet 40 kitchens on a promise, and the board sees proof before money moves.

options.text: Remind her how hard switching would be
options.feedback: True, but it sounds like a threat. Business buyers remember who made them feel trapped, and they act on it at the next renewal.

cards.title: Say you chose the pilot. Then week four goes wrong.
body: Label printing fails on older printers in two pilot kitchens. The fix needs two more weeks, past the date you promised.

options.text: Call the director today with the problem and a new date
options.feedback: Uncomfortable now, but she hears it from you, not from her cooks. Bad news told early can build more trust than a smooth project.

options.text: Work weekends quietly and hope to hit the date
options.feedback: If you make it, nobody knows. If you miss, she learns you hid a problem during a trial meant to test you.

options.text: Launch on time with labels switched off in those two kitchens
options.feedback: You keep the date, but two kitchens go without the part cooks wanted most. They'll tell the director anyway.

cards.title: Renewal signed, and a feature everyone can use.
body: The fix shipped two weeks late. The pilot kitchens kept using the labels, and the group renewed all 40 locations at the same price.
Within a month, three other restaurant customers switched on allergen flags. The custom dashboard was never built, and nobody missed it.

image.label: Prep containers with printed allergen labels in a busy kitchen
image.brief: 레스토랑 주방 선반에 알레르기 라벨이 붙은 재료 용기들이 줄지어 있고, 요리사가 태블릿으로 레시피의 알레르기 표시를 확인하는 장면. 배경에 다른 식당 세 곳이 작은 아이콘으로 연결됨. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Not every request should become a standard feature.
body: This worked because the need was common. Every restaurant handles allergens. Some requests really are one customer's quirk. Then price the work clearly, or say no.

The same call faces a bakery whose hotel client wants a recipe only that hotel buys. And watch the dependence itself: when one customer is 30% of revenue, every request feels like a threat. **More customers** is the lasting fix.

cards.title: Treat a big customer's request as a buying decision, not an order.
body: Each step used one idea from this unit:
list: **Ask first:** the buyer, the users and the signer wanted different things (buyers vs users, buying committees)
**Build for many:** a one-off keeps costing long after it ships (total cost of ownership)
**Pilot:** shrink the buyer's risk, not just the price (risk in business buying)
**Call early:** bad news told first protects the relationship (trust and relationships)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your biggest customer's last request. Write down who asked, who would use it, and who signs.
